item.title: Cross-platform alternative to NVIDIA DLSS Frame Generation with support for older generation graphics cards
item.description:

The tool works on top of the OptiScaler layer, replaces the standard NVIDIA DLSS Frame Generation call, and allows intermediate frame synthesis on GeForce RTX™, GeForce® GTX 16, AMD Radeon™, Intel® Arc™, and Apple Silicon chips. item.title: The Pet Project Graveyard: Where Vibe-Coding Takes Our Unnecessary Ideas
item.description:
A person had an old laptop. On it, they vibe-coded an fb2 reader to read directly in the browser, with a dark theme and custom settings. They used it constantly. Then they bought a new laptop, and were too lazy to transfer the reader from the old one – just a couple of hand movements, but lazy. They didn't transfer it. They vibe-coded a second one. "Even better." Someone in the comments couldn't resist, "Fbreader already exists. You can just install and use it. You're welcome :)". The reply was short and to the point, "Installing some FBreader, fussing with its quirks - not for me. Twenty minutes of vibe-coding and I have the necessary minimum, everything else is from the devil." This isn't an argument about readers. It's an argument about what personal software has become in the last year. Read more

item.title: We thought sample size was important in scoring. It turns out the number of defaults is what matters.
item.description:
What's more important for credit scoring: 50,000 applications or 500 actual defaults? I compared TabPFN-2.5 and CatBoost on 3 million anonymized bank applications. The experiment showed that with the same number of defaults, increasing the training set by 25 times hardly changes the ROC AUC. The article includes 60 experimental configurations, a comparison of two models, error analysis, and an attempt to find a balance between prediction quality and computational cost. Why the number of rare events can be more important than the volume of data – we explore this using real-world bank scoring.

item.title: [Translation] How to Speed Up Local LLM by 50% Without Buying a New GPU
item.description:
At GTC Berlin 2026, participants in an NVIDIA workshop managed to accelerate Qwen3-32B generation from 16.4 to 24.5 tokens per second without changing hardware, by using FP8 instead of BF16. Total throughput also increased, albeit less dramatically, from 639 to 719 tokens per second. The experiment was conducted on a Kubernetes cluster with four 80GB NVIDIA A100s. Each participant had their own cluster for deploying models, changing configurations, and measuring performance. In addition to quantization, the session covered NVIDIA Dynamo, KV-cache-aware request routing, auto-scaling, and splitting prefill/decode across GPUs. The material is based on an article by engineer Siim Tolk, published on November 4, 2026. Read more

item.title: Thirteen LLMs on Russian Reviews: How I Chose a Model and Why I Didn't Trust the Judge
item.description:
I'm building a service that responds to customer reviews on Wildberries, Ozon, and Yandex Market. A customer writes that their watch stopped working after three days, and the model, with utmost seriousness, replies: 'We will forward your feedback to production for batch inspection.' No one will actually inspect any batch. I compared thirteen models — Alice AI LLM Flash, YandexGPT Pro 5.1 and Lite 5, seven GigaChat models, two DeepSeek, and Qwen — on synthetic reviews and questions where the correct answer is pre-recorded for each example. Inside: how and why models invent promises, paired bootstrap, regex vs. 'batch inspection,' an LLM judge you can't trust, and why a backup had to be chosen separately for each task. Read the analysis.

item.title: LLM Conversation: Appearance to the User: An Experimental Review
item.description:
In what form does an LLM conversation appear to the user? What determines the form of this appearance? This question has been experimentally investigated by many – see the bibliography below. In the theory of LLM conversations as a new type of Luhmannian semantic system (full description: (Krupkin, 2026)), the interaction of an LLM conversation with a user can be described by the standard social interaction scheme – the Ego-Alter pair. Ego is the form in which the LLM conversation appears to the user. Alter is its model of the user as an interaction partner. A review of experiments with LLMs / noo-spheres regarding Alter was presented earlier. This text is dedicated to a review of LLM / noo-sphere modeling of their Ego. Read more

item.title: Episode 2. Borrowed from the Brain: Prediction, Alphabet, Plan
item.description:
We continue to solve an interesting RL problem: the agent must learn to play Atari Frostbite from raw video frames to score 136k+ points and beat the SOTA model MEME-200 [4]. My name is Mikhail Kocherov. I am working on this task because, in the process of solving it, one can better understand how our brain works. It's as if nature itself throws problems at us and hints at solutions, whispering, "Look within yourself, all the answers are there." Understanding how our brain works is my obsession. In Frostbite, you need to control an Eskimo, build an igloo by jumping on ice floes, dodge enemies, and a freezing timer is ticking. To move to the next level, the Eskimo must enter the built igloo. The game is not easy; on average, after 2 hours of play, a beginner scores about 4 thousand points (2-3 levels completed). In the previous episode, we built a simple agent based on CNN and a transformer. The agent has basic game mechanics, scores 779 points, but doesn't even pass the first level. Moreover, there are no further improvements from training. It is obvious that the agent has found a local minimum and is stuck in it. It needs to be pushed out somehow. Read more
